title: Riding the wave with mindfulness
summary: Urges rise, peak, and fall. Mindfulness is how you watch them pass.

blocks.text: An urge feels permanent in the moment, but it isn't. Like a wave, it builds, crests, and falls — usually within 15 to 30 minutes if you don't feed it.
Notice instead of fight
Fighting an urge often makes it louder. Mindfulness offers a different move: turn toward it with curiosity, name what's happening, and let it be there without acting.

items: Name it: "This is an urge. It will pass."
Locate it in your body — chest, stomach, hands.
Breathe into that spot, slow and low.
Watch the intensity rise and fall like a wave.

blocks.text: You are not your urges. You're the person noticing them — and that person gets to choose what happens next.

title: Your strengths are still there
summary: Compulsive behaviour doesn't erase who you are.

blocks.text: Shame tells a simple, cruel story: that the behaviour is proof you're broken. It isn't. The qualities that make you you — kindness, humour, effort, care — didn't go anywhere.
Find the evidence
Think of a time you showed up for someone, kept a promise, or did something hard. That person is still you. Recovery isn't becoming someone new — it's letting who you already are lead.

items: Name three strengths a friend would say you have.
Recall one recent moment each showed up.
Notice: the part of you reading this wants to grow. That's a strength too.

title: Affirmations that don't feel fake
summary: Skip the hollow slogans. Try honest, believable statements.

blocks.text: "I am amazing" can feel like a lie when you're low — and your brain rejects lies. Effective affirmations are believable and process-focused, not grandiose.

items: "I'm learning, and slips are part of learning."
"I can do one small hard thing right now."
"I've gotten through hard moments before."
"I'm allowed to be a work in progress."

blocks.text: Say the one that feels most true today — out loud if you can. Repeat it when the harsh inner voice gets loud.

title: Real intimacy vs. the counterfeit
summary: Why porn can leave you lonelier, and what genuine closeness needs.

blocks.text: Compulsive use often promises connection but delivers isolation. Real intimacy is built on things a screen can't give: being known, being vulnerable, and being present with another person.
What real closeness is made of

items: Presence — actually being here, not half-elsewhere.
Vulnerability — letting yourself be seen, flaws and all.
Reciprocity — two people, both giving and receiving.
Time — closeness grows slowly and can't be rushed.

blocks.text: Rebuilding intimacy can feel awkward at first. That awkwardness is normal — it's the feeling of a real skill coming back online.

title: Saying what you need
summary: Simple tools for honest, non-blaming conversations.

blocks.text: Most conflict isn't about the topic — it's about feeling unheard. A few small shifts make it far more likely you'll actually be understood.
Try "I" statements
"You never listen" invites defence. "I feel unheard when I'm interrupted" invites a response. Name the feeling and the specific situation, not the character flaw.

items: I feel ___ (emotion)
when ___ (specific situation, not "you always")
and I'd appreciate ___ (a clear, doable request).

blocks.text: You can't control how someone responds — only how clearly and kindly you show up. That's enough.

title: Consent, respect, and connection
summary: Consent isn't a hurdle — it's the ground healthy intimacy stands on.

blocks.text: Consent is an ongoing, enthusiastic, freely-given yes — not the absence of a no. It can be withdrawn at any time, by anyone, for any reason.

items: Freely given — no pressure, guilt, or intoxication.
Reversible — anyone can change their mind, anytime.
Informed and specific — yes to one thing isn't yes to all.
Enthusiastic — look for a real yes, not a reluctant one.

blocks.text: Treating consent as central isn't a mood-killer — it builds the trust and safety that real closeness needs.

title: What anxiety is really doing
summary: Your alarm system is trying to protect you — even when it's wrong.

blocks.text: Anxiety is your body's alarm system firing. It's uncomfortable, but it isn't dangerous — it's a false alarm, not a fire. Understanding that takes some of its power away.
The link with urges
Anxiety is a common trigger: the discomfort makes the quick escape of a compulsive behaviour tempting. Learning to soothe the alarm directly removes the reason to escape.

items: Slow exhale — longer out-breath than in-breath calms the body.
Ground with 5-4-3-2-1 (see the emergency tools).
Release physical tension with the muscle-relaxation session here.
Remind yourself: "This is uncomfortable, not dangerous."

title: When you can't feel motivated, act first
summary: In low mood, action comes before motivation — not after.

blocks.text: Low mood whispers "wait until you feel like it." But motivation usually follows action, not the other way around. This is the core idea behind behavioural activation, a well-studied approach for low mood.
Schedule small, doable things
Pick one small activity that used to give you a sense of pleasure or accomplishment, and do it — regardless of how you feel. Then notice your mood before and after.

items: Make it tiny: a 10-minute walk, one dish washed, a text to a friend.
Schedule it for a specific time today.
Rate your mood 0–10 before and after — evidence beats the whisper.
Stack small wins. They add up faster than they feel like they do.

blocks.text: If low mood is heavy, persistent, or you're having thoughts of harming yourself, please talk to a doctor or reach the crisis resources in this app. You deserve real support.

title: Small changes for better sleep
summary: Sleep and recovery feed each other. A few habits move the needle.

blocks.text: Poor sleep drains willpower and worsens mood — both make urges harder to ride out. Late-night scrolling is also a common trigger, so protecting your sleep protects your recovery.
Wind-down basics

items: Keep a consistent wake time — even on weekends.
No screens in bed; charge your phone across the room.
Dim the lights an hour before sleep.
Cut caffeine after early afternoon.
If you can't sleep after 20 minutes, get up and do something calm.

blocks.text: Try the wind-down session here as part of your bedtime routine — the same practice each night trains your body to expect rest.
